newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Analysts fear Sharon role in Israel economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Analysts fear Sharon role in Israel economic policy.

text.p: Will Ariel Sharon, the man most likely to become Israel's next finance minister, be the budget-busting, interventionist bulldozer his reputation points to?

That is the question facing the financial markets as they await Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet shake-up, which is expected to land the controversial ex-general in the top economic policy-making post.

"He believes much more than previous finance ministers in government involvement in the economy," said Yoram Gabbai, a former Treasury revenues director and now a fund manager. "He doesn't believe in a liberal economy."
Sharon's reputation as a bulldozer ready to roll over the opposition to implement a decision was acquired in his army years and enhanced when he was housing minister in the early 1990s.

"He is ideologically inclined towards government involvement in stabilising the economy. His tendency is to look at the geopolitical situation in terms of territory," said Amiram Gonen, director of the Florsheimer Institute for Policy Studies in Jerusalem.

As housing minister, Sharon built tens of thousands of houses for a flood of immigrants entering Israel from the former Soviet Union. But the homes he built, offering contractors generous government aid, were mainly in the West Bank and on Israel's periphery, where there were few jobs and services.
Many of the homes were left empty and when the Labour government came to power in 1994, the public sector building programme was cut short.

Israel's Treasury preferred a more free-market solution to absorbing the wave of immigrants, but Sharon prevailed in the matter of housing, recalled Gonen. He saw the immigrants as a means of dispersing Israel's population, even if it was at great cost to the budget.
"For Sharon the geopolitical perspective has the edge over the economic perspective," said Gonen.

With immigration down to a fraction of its level in the early 1990s, Gonen said Sharon would see his new geopolitical priority as strengthening the Israeli presence in the West Bank before completion final status talks in the region with the Palestinians. He is likely also to spend money bootstrapping the economies of the periphery to ensure that the immigrants who settled there remain.
"Today he thinks that this is the time to do as much as we can in the West Bank, even if it means enlarging the budget deficit to accomplish it," said Gonen.
That would mark a sea change at the Treasury, where Meridor was a forceful advocate of budgetary restraint.

But Gabbai said he believed Sharon would surprise his critics. "I expect him to keep a tight fiscal policy. I don't think there'll be a big difference between him and other finance ministers" who have taken their cue from the ministry's budget division, he said.
In an interview in the daily newspaper Haaretz on Tuesday, Stanley Fischer, an official at the International Monetary Fund in Washington, advised Sharon to take on the cause of budgetary restraint.
"A quick cut in the budget to make clear to everyone that he plans to act differently as finance minister than he did as industry minister and housing minister," Fischer recommended.

Gabbai is less confident Sharon will continue to pursue Israel's policy of economic and trade liberalisation, noting that in his term as industry and trade minister in the late 1980s Sharon opposed a plan to ease import barriers.
"I expect to see in the Sharon era an effort to slow Israel's economic liberalisation," Gabbai said. "He'll keep (existing) agreements but progress won't be as fast as in the last six years."

Sharon's tenure as infrastructure minister over the last year has been marked by uncharacterisitc quiet, but most analysts said they did not believe that signaled a new kinder, gentler Sharon. "He's a bulldozer, don't worry," Gabbai said.
